resources.string: A spectral darkroom on your phone
Spektrafilm renders your photos through a physically-modelled film stock and darkroom print — spectrum-accurate, not a preset filter.
Three steps to a finished photograph
Open a JPEG, HEIC or RAW/DNG from your gallery or the file picker.
Start from a preset, then keep or change the film stock and print paper.
Adjust strength, exposure and grain, then save at full resolution to your gallery.
Decoding, film simulation and export all run on this phone. Photos are never uploaded and no account is needed.
Spectral film simulation on your phone — film modeling powered by spektrafilm.

Spektrafilm is a physically-based spectral film simulator. Unlike a simple filter or a look-up table, it models the real analog pipeline: a virtual negative is exposed to your photo\'s light, developed in a chemical bath, optionally enlarged onto print paper in a darkroom, and scanned back to a digital file — all driven by measured spectral data from real film stocks.
The result is a faithful reproduction of color, grain, halation, and dye chemistry that matches what you would get in a real darkroom — not an approximation.
Film modeling powered by spektrafilm (Andrea Volpato).
Tap the open button (top-left of the editor) to pick an image.
Choose a JPEG or HEIC from your gallery for quick results.
For the truest film rendering, open a RAW or DNG file. The app decodes RAW files through LibRaw to a linear, scene-referred image — the same starting point real film would have.
If you don\'t have a photo handy, tap \"Demo image\" to load the built-in test image.
EXIF orientation is read automatically: portrait shots and rotated RAW files will appear upright in the preview without you doing anything.
The editor is designed like a professional photo editing app. From top to bottom:

Pinned preview — your photo, rendered live with the current settings, fills the top portion of the screen. A status pill in the corner shows when a render is in progress and how long the last render took. Tap the photo once to hide every control and see it full-bleed, and tap again to bring them back. Press and hold the photo to see it unedited, and let go to come back; double-tap to zoom to 100%, pinch to zoom freely, drag to pan.

Histogram — displayed over the preview so you can judge exposure and clipping. A blue wedge in its top-left corner means shadows are being crushed to black; a red wedge in its top-right means highlights are blowing out. Neither appears for a stray pixel or two — it takes about one pixel in a thousand.

Sliders — while you drag one, the panel fades almost away so you can see the whole photograph, and the value floats in the top-right corner. Each value sits in a pill: tap it to type an exact number, drag it sideways to adjust ten times finer than the track allows, and double-tap it to send that one parameter back to its default. A pill with a ring around it is a parameter you have moved away from its default. When a whole group holds changes, a Reset button appears at the top of its panel.

Stage bar — five stages along the bottom: Look, Film, Print, Scan and Finish. These are the stages the engine actually simulates, in order: you start from a look, expose the negative, print it, scan the print, and grade the result.

Tapping a stage opens it and shows that stage\'s parameter groups as scrollable text labels just above the stage bar. A dot on a stage or a group means something in it differs from the neutral defaults, so you can see at a glance which parts of the pipeline are acting on your photo. The groups, by stage, are:
Swipe the panel downward, or tap the open stage again, to dismiss it and return to the full preview.
open a photo, open RAW, demo image, histogram, reset edits
load a built-in or saved parameter set
film stock, print paper, exposure, Auto-exposure
grain amount, scale, sublayer mixing, 100% magnifier
lens flare / glare (print path, off by default)
developer options and advanced engine flags
master and per-channel curves applied after the scan
local adjustments painted or shaped over part of the frame
output color space (sRGB, Adobe RGB, ProPhoto, Rec.2020, etc.)
Top bar — open a photo, undo, redo, the "Save to gallery" primary button, and an overflow menu with Settings and About on narrow screens. On wider screens Settings and About are direct actions.

Settings holds colour management, export defaults and the app\'s diagnostics. Export defaults only seed a new Export sheet; the format, size, colour space and file name you pick there apply to that one export.
Start here to find the right film character for your photo:

Open the Film stage and pick a film stock from the Film picker — %1$d profiles are available, grouped as color negative, slide, motion-picture and print film. Each entry shows the stock\'s ISO, colour balance and a one-line note on its character.
If you want a printed look (negative→enlarger→paper), also select a print paper in the Print picker within Simulation. Leave it at its default for a direct scan-of-the-negative result.

Adjust the exposure slider to brighten or darken the simulated exposure. Alternatively, tap Auto to let the app meter the scene for you. Auto-exposure meters to a mid-grey target and offers 7 metering patterns (center-weighted, matrix, spot, and more) in a pop-up list.

For a fast starting point, open the Look stage — it opens the preset list directly. %1$d built-in, researched film-to-print looks are available. Tapping one applies its full parameter set immediately, with no separate Apply step, then fine-tune from there.
Several tools are available directly in the editor:
90° rotate — the rotate button in the tool row at the bottom of the preview rotates your photo 90° clockwise. The rotation applies to the preview, the export, and the grain magnifier.

Crop — the crop button in the same tool row opens the interactive crop overlay. Drag the corner and edge handles to crop freely, or tap one of the aspect ratio presets (1:1, 4:3, 3:2, 16:9, etc.) to lock the ratio.
Before / after compare — the compare button in the tool row below the preview toggles a draggable split between the original and the simulated result, so you can judge the effect.
100% grain magnifier — the magnifier button in the same tool row. Shows a 1:1 crop of the grain texture so you can check the grain scale and character before exporting at full resolution.

Profile curve browser — in the Simulation category, tap the film or paper name to open the curve browser. It shows that stock\'s spectral sensitivity, characteristic (H-D) density curves, and dye density spectra.
When a RAW or DNG file is loaded, the RAW WB category becomes active. It gives you control over how LibRaw interprets the raw sensor data:
Mode — choose As-shot (uses the camera\'s recorded white balance), Daylight, or Tungsten for a preset. Select Custom to enter your own values.
Temperature and Tint sliders — available in Custom mode to dial in a precise white balance. Changing either slider re-decodes the RAW preview automatically.
Reset — returns the white balance to the camera\'s as-shot setting.
For JPEG or HEIC sources the RAW WB category is hidden, since the white balance is already baked into those files.
All edits are non-destructive. Here is what that means in practice:
Your original file is never changed. The app only reads it.
Every adjustment is stored as a recipe (a small JSON sidecar) keyed to that specific source image.
When you reopen the same image later, the recipe is loaded automatically and the simulation re-renders exactly where you left off.
The recipe is re-applied at full resolution when you export, so your preview at a smaller size and the exported file at full resolution are the same look.
When you are happy with the look, tap the "Save to gallery" button in the top bar to open the export sheet.
The export options live in this export sheet:

Format — choose from 8-bit JPEG, 8-bit PNG, 16-bit TIFF, 16-bit PNG, or Google Ultra HDR (gain-map JPEG, on supported devices). 16-bit TIFF and 16-bit PNG preserve the full dynamic range of the simulation and always export at full resolution.

Size — full resolution, Large (4096 px), Medium (2048 px), Small (1024 px), or a custom long edge. A custom edge accepts 256–16384 px; leave it empty for the original size. A non-numeric or out-of-range value is flagged inline and disables "Save to gallery".

JPEG quality — a 10–100 slider for JPEG and Ultra HDR exports. Keep GPS / location — OFF by default for privacy. Turn it on if you want GPS coordinates copied from the source EXIF into the exported file.

File name — optional. Chinese characters, accented letters and other Unicode letters are kept; path separators, emoji and characters a file name does not need are removed, and the sheet previews the actual file name with its extension. If nothing usable remains, a dated Spektrafilm name is used automatically. The exported file is saved to Pictures/Spektrafilm on your device. Camera metadata (make, model, lens, exposure settings) from the source image is copied into the exported file\'s EXIF automatically.
Judge film looks in a darkened room. Film character is subtle and ambient light on the screen will flatten your perception of it.
Use RAW input for the most accurate result. JPEG files have already been processed by the camera\'s tone curve, white balance, and sharpening, which changes how the simulation perceives the scene.
Export to 16-bit TIFF or 16-bit PNG when you plan to do further editing. This keeps the full precision of the simulation for later adjustments.
Auto-exposure meters to mid-grey. If your subject is lighter or darker than mid-grey you may want to nudge the exposure slider manually afterward.
Grain is stochastic (random). The preview may look slightly different each time you render; the export is always the definitive full-resolution version.

Film modeling powered by spektrafilm (Andrea Volpato). The science, the film-stock profiles, and the spectral LUTs are Andrea\'s work — Spektrafilm is a native Android port of that engine, verified bit-exact against the original.
UI inspired by Image Toolbox (T8RIN). Colour math from colour-science. RAW decoding via LibRaw. Free software under the GPLv3.
Applied immediately. Follows the system language by default.
Off by default (Android 12+ only). On: derive the palette from your wallpaper. Off: use the built-in warm darkroom palette.
Applied on the next launch, when you open a new photo. Per-image edits and presets still override these.
Long edge of the interactive preview, in pixels.
Long edge of the fast frame drawn while a slider is being dragged, before the crisp render lands. Lower tracks your finger more closely; higher previews the final result more faithfully.
Applies when you return to the editor. An export sheet that is already open keeps its own settings.
Off: strip GPS from exports (recommended). Other EXIF (camera, exposure, date) is always kept.

Render the fit preview instantly on the GPU (a 3D LUT of the current look) instead of a ~1s CPU render per edit. This toggle never affects export. Off by default: the current surface can stutter or overlap the controls while panels animate — being reworked.

Run the film simulation\'s scan stage on the GPU for interactive previews — more accurate than the preview LUT and verified against the CPU engine on this device at first use, with automatic CPU fallback. This toggle never affects export. Applies on the next return to the editor.

Run more of the export on the GPU at full resolution. The colour stages are checked against the CPU engine on this device and fall back to CPU automatically if they ever drift. Grain and viewing glare are different: they are re-drawn with a faster random generator, so the noise pattern will not match the default engine — same amount and character of grain, different speckle. Repeat exports on this device stay identical. For an export that matches the default engine exactly, leave this off. Off by default. Independent of the preview toggle.
Nothing is uploaded automatically. Reports include app/device version, redact paths, URIs and image metadata, and keep the last crash for at most 7 days. Copy or Share is always an explicit action.
